statement: Egyptian hieroglyphs are DECIPHERED. The Rosetta Stone was discovered 1799; Thomas Young published a partial decipherment (Encyclopaedia Britannica supplement, 1819) correctly intuiting that cartouches enclosed royal names and proposing phonetic values for 13 signs, but limited to foreign (Ptolemy/Cleopatra) names and never generalized. Jean-François Champollion's 1822 Lettre à M. Dacier was the decisive breakthrough: he recognized the phonetic principle was NOT limited to foreign names but applied generally to native Egyptian words, meaning hieroglyphic writing was fundamentally a mixed phonetic-and-ideographic system throughout — the distinction that separates "Champollion alone solved it" (an oversimplification) from "Young essentially solved it first" (also not accurate); modern historiography credits Champollion with the decisive, generalizing breakthrough while acknowledging Young's real contributory role. Actual pronunciation of Egyptian remains substantially a modern scholarly reconstruction, since hieroglyphic writing omits vowels in most cases — a genuine limitation distinct from the script/grammar being unread.
